symptoms: Global route overflow histogram shows >5% overflow concentrated in <10% of gcells, especially near macro corners and channels, not spread uniformly.
Detail-route DRC count after first routing iteration is >1000, with the majority being 'short' violations in the same macro-adjacent bins.
Placement utilization in congested areas is >85% (at 28nm) or >75% (at 7nm) while average utilization is under 70%, indicating local density peaks.
Route completion fails with 'unroutable' error after multiple iterations, yet the total wirelength is within expected bounds.

candidate_causes.cause: Hard macro placements (SRAMs/PHYs) create narrow channels with insufficient routing tracks for the number of signals crossing.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Overlay the macro boundary map with the routing overflow map; if overflow bins align exactly with macro-to-macro gaps and are absent elsewhere, confirm macro channel blockage.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Shift macros to widen the most critical channels by 5–10% of their width, or reassign signal pin layers to use higher metal layers exiting the channel.
candidate_causes.fix_cost: hours to days (depending on timing impact)

candidate_causes.cause: Standard-cell placement density too high in a region due to an overly aggressive area target, causing local grid shortage.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Run a cell-density heatmap and overlay with overflow map; if high density >80% correlates with overflow, confirm. Check total utilization is not the issue.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add placement blockages to spread cells into adjacent less-congested regions, or increase chip area slightly.

candidate_causes.cause: Power grid stripes (at higher metal layers) and signal routing blockages consume a significant portion of the routing tracks, reducing available wire resources.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Compare available tracks per layer (subtracting power grid/blockages) against the global route demand per layer; if demand exceeds available tracks on layers where stripes are dense, this is the cause.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Reduce the number of power stripes in that region (if IR drop allows), or move blockages to lower-utilization layers.

candidate_causes.cause: Floorplan aspect ratio too extreme (e.g., very long and narrow), forcing long global wires through a narrow middle corridor.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Examine the overflow map for a single dense band across the center; check the aspect ratio and wirelength distribution for that corridor.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Re‑floorplan to a more square aspect ratio, or add a reserved routing corridor with higher track count.

candidate_causes.cause: High fanout net clustering creates many local branches, causing congestion in small areas.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Look at failing gcells and identify if a small number of high-fanout nets (e.g., resets/scan-enables) account for >50% of the overflow in those bins.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert buffers to split the fanout and redistribute wires, or route that net on a dedicated higher layer.

ordering_rationale: Veterans check macro placement first (highest prior probability in 28nm/7nm blocks with many hard macros), then power-grid interference, then density, then floorplan shape, then fanout nets – because each subsequent check requires more simulation overhead but targets less common cases.
classic_trap: Misdiagnosing as a placement-density problem and respreading cells, when the root cause is actually macro channel blockage – respreading worsens the issue by moving cells away from macros but does nothing to open the routing channels.

symptoms: WNS (Worst Negative Slack) between -100ps and -500ps on a few dozen paths, while TNS (Total Negative Slack) is moderate (~10-50ns), and the failing paths share a common clock-gating cell or a common point in the clock tree.
WNS is large (> -1ns) and TNS is huge (>500ns), with thousands of failing paths spread across unrelated hierarchical modules and data paths.
Failing paths have a very high net delay contribution (>60% of total path delay) despite short logical levels, indicating slow wires.
Failing paths all originate from the same launch clock domain and capture into the same capture clock domain (or cross-domain) with marginal positive slack on all other paths.

candidate_causes.cause: Clock skew imbalance between launch and capture flops – local clock tree insertion delays vary by >50ps due to uneven buffer placements.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Extract clock arrival times at the launch and capture flops for the failing paths; if the skew (launch - capture) is positive and >50ps larger than the budget, confirm. Check the clock tree report for balance.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Rebalance the clock tree by adjusting buffer sizing or placement near the capture flops to reduce skew.

candidate_causes.cause: Excessive logic depth (number of cell levels) in the data path, causing a long cell delay contribution.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: List the cell delay contributions per failing path; if the average logic level is >10 for a 28nm process at 1GHz, and net delay is normal, this is the cause.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Restructure RTL to pipeline the combinational logic, or swap in faster (but larger) standard cells.

candidate_causes.cause: Physical placement separation between the launching and capturing flops is large, leading to high wire RC delay.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Measure the Manhattan distance between flop pairs on failing paths; if the average distance >200µm (for a small block) and net delay dominates, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Place the flops closer together via a placement constraint, or use intermediate buffers with repeaters.

candidate_causes.cause: Constraint error: a multicycle path or false path is mis-constrained, leading to an overly tight setup check.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check the SDC: if the failing paths are between clock domains with asynchronous relationship or are known designer-intended multicycle paths (e.g., write/read of SRAM), confirm by design spec.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add the correct multicycle or false-path constraint, or adjust the clock phase.

candidate_causes.cause: Cross-talk noise from adjacent aggressor nets couples into the data path, increasing effective delay on wire segments.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Run a signal integrity (SI) delay analysis; if the SI-induced delay adds >50ps to the failing paths, confirm. Look for parallel long wires.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Shield the victim net, increase spacing, or skew aggressors to reduce coupling.

ordering_rationale: Check SDC first (cheapest, quickest to fix), then clock skew (common at high frequency), then placement distance, then logic depth, then SI – because SI analysis is expensive and often a secondary effect.
classic_trap: Assuming it is a logic-depth problem and rewriting RTL, when the actual issue is a 50ps clock skew imbalance that can be fixed by a local clock tree adjustment in a few hours.

symptoms: Hold violations appear on hundreds of short paths, with negative slack typically between -50ps and -200ps, clustered near the same clock domains or within the same physical region.
All failing paths have very low logic depth (1–2 cells) and very short wire lengths, but they exhibit large clock skew (capture clock arriving earlier than launch clock).
Hold violations appear only after fixing setup, because inserting buffers for setup increases wire delay but also increases clock skew.
Violations are localized to flops that have undergone useful-skew adjustments during setup fixing.

candidate_causes.cause: Uneven clock tree skew – the capture flop receives the clock significantly earlier than the launch flop (negative skew), leaving insufficient hold margin.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Extract the local skew between launch and capture clock pins; if skew (capture - launch) < -100ps for most failing paths, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add a delay buffer on the capture clock path to delay the clock arrival, or rebalance the tree.

candidate_causes.cause: Excessive clock jitter or uncertainty margin added in the SDC, artificially shrinking the hold window.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check the clock uncertainty value applied for hold (often 0 or negative); if it is positive, it may be too aggressive. Compare with the datasheet.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Reduce or remove the hold uncertainty if it was overly conservative (or ensure it matches reality).

candidate_causes.cause: Data path is too short – minimal combinational delay between two flops in the same clock domain, leaving no margin for local skew.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Examine the path report; if the data path has only a clock-to-Q delay of the launch flop plus a single buffer and a short wire, and the total delay < skew + hold requirement, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert a delay buffer (or two) in the data path to add delay, or insert a clock delay on the capture clock.

candidate_causes.cause: Clock gating cell inserted in the capture clock path without balancing its delay against non-gated paths.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check if the failing flops share a clock-gating cell that is present only on the capture side; compare with flops that pass – those without the gate have no violation.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add a matching delay element on the ungated clock paths to balance the clock tree, or remove the gating if not needed.

candidate_causes.cause: Cross-die or on-chip variation (OCV) mismodeled – using a single global derate instead of stage-based derates makes hold look worse.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Recalculate hold slack using custom OCV derates (e.g., path-based) and see if violations disappear; also check if physical distance causes mismatch.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Use more accurate OCV derate tables or implement advanced OCV (AOCV) coefficients.

ordering_rationale: Check clock skew first (most common cause in high-frequency designs), then SDC uncertainty (very cheap), then data path length, then gating cells, then OCV – because OCV tuning is a longer iterative process.
classic_trap: Adding a large delay buffer to every failing path, which then creates new setup violations on the same paths or on nearby paths, entering a fix-loops cycle.

symptoms: Static IR drop report shows >5% VDD drop in core regions, but dynamic IR drop (with toggle activity) shows >10% peak drop, causing timing violations on paths that pass static analysis.
Timing failures are highly activity-dependent – only occur during certain functional patterns (e.g., vector scan), not during static timing analysis.
Multiple cells in a contiguous region show simultaneous slowdown, visible as grouping of setup violations in the same physical area with similar path delays.
Power rails show high local current density (exceeding 100 mA/µm) in electromigration checks near high-switching macros.

candidate_causes.cause: Insufficient on-chip power grid density – the metal mesh is too sparse for the peak current demand, creating local voltage sag.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Overlay the IR drop map with the power grid pitch; if the drop is maximal at the center of the grid tiles and reduces near stripes, confirm. Run a grid resistance extraction.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add more power stripes or increase metal width in the grid (if area allows), or add decoupling capacitors.

candidate_causes.cause: Excessive simultaneous switching activity (SSA) in a small area – a large number of flops or clock gates toggle at the same clock edge, drawing a large current spike.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Run a vector-based dynamic IR analysis with the maximum-toggling functional pattern; if the drop peak coincides with the clock edge and the toggling cell density is high, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add local decoupling capacitance, stagger clock gating enables, or reduce the number of flops per clock buffer.

candidate_causes.cause: Package/PCB power delivery impedance too high, causing AC droop that is not captured by on-chip DC analysis.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check the board-level PDN impedance and compare with the chip's current step response; if the droop frequency matches board resonance, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add more package decoupling capacitors, adjust package via count, or change on-chip decap distribution.

candidate_causes.cause: Clock tree buffers are concentrated in one area (due to floorplan) and draw a large current simultaneously, causing a hot spot.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Run a per-instance current map; if the highest drop region coincides with clock buffer density > average by 5x, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Spread clock buffers across the chip, or use multiple smaller clock trees to reduce peak current.

candidate_causes.cause: Missing or insufficient power vias connecting the on-chip grid to the package bumps, increasing local resistance.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Extract the via density map; if the drop occurs near regions with fewer vias per area, confirm by comparing with bump map.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add more vias in the floorplan, or repartition the power bump assignment.

ordering_rationale: Check on-chip grid density first (simplest to spot with static analysis), then dynamic activity via vector simulation (next likely), then via/bump integrity, then package – because package fixes are expensive and require cross-team coordination.
classic_trap: Treating a dynamic IR drop issue as a static one and thickening the grid everywhere, which wastes area and does not solve the current spike caused by simultaneous toggling.

symptoms: Clock skew histogram shows a long tail >100ps beyond target, with a small subset of flops (e.g., <5%) having much larger insertion delays than the rest.
Clock transition (slew) violations appear at sinks, with slew >500ps at 28nm (or >200ps at 7nm) on many clock endpoints, often clustered near macros.
Timing reports show a consistent 'clock path pessimism' that varies widely between paths, indicating clock tree imbalance.
Post‑CTS setup violations are uniformly worse than pre‑CTS estimated slacks by a constant factor (e.g., all slacks degrade by 100ps), suggesting a systematic clock latency issue.

candidate_causes.cause: Uneven distribution of clock sinks due to floorplan – a dense cluster of flops requires many buffers, leading to long branches to sparse areas.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Plot the flop density heatmap and overlay with clock tree buffer placement; if sparse areas have very few buffers but long wires, while dense areas have many, confirm imbalance.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert dummy buffers or route the clock spine to balance the tree, or adjust floorplan to distribute flops more evenly.

candidate_causes.cause: Macros (SRAMs/PHYs) block clock routing, forcing detours that add excessive wire delay to certain sinks.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check the physical path of the clock net; if it must route around a large macro, and the delayed sinks are exactly those on the far side, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add a dedicated clock channel around the macro, or use a higher metal layer to jump over it, or split the clock tree into two separate balanced trees.

candidate_causes.cause: Clock gating cells inserted without regard to delay balancing – some gated branches have significantly different insertion delays than ungated ones.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Compare insertion delays of gated vs ungated sinks that share the same root; if the difference exceeds 100ps consistently, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Add delay compensation on the faster branches, or replace clock gating with enable flops that have balanced clock paths.

candidate_causes.cause: Incorrect clock tree synthesis constraints – target skew or target latency set too aggressively, causing the tool to insert many buffers that create other issues.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Review the CTS constraint file; if the target skew is <20ps (unrealistic for the process) or the target latency is very tight, suspect over‑constraint.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Relax the target skew to a feasible value (e.g., 50ps for 28nm) and rerun CTS.

candidate_causes.cause: Different clock domains routed with different buffer types or different metal layers, causing systematic skew between domains.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Compare insertion delays of the two domains; if one is consistently >200ps longer, and they share the same root, check the buffer cell library and layer assignment.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Harmonize the buffer type and route layer assignments for all clocks, or add offset compensation.

ordering_rationale: Check floorplan/macro blockage first (most common in large blocks), then clock gating balance, then constraints, then per‑domain differences – because floorplan issues are visually obvious and yield high impact fixes.
classic_trap: Re‑running CTS with more iterations and hoping the skew improves, without first identifying that the root cause is a physical blockage that no amount of buffer insertion can overcome.

symptoms: After detailed routing, the DRC report shows >500 violations, predominantly of the 'short' and 'spacing' types on a single metal layer (e.g., M4).
Antenna violations appear on a large number of nets, typically those connected to gate inputs of standard cells, concentrated in certain regions.
Via density violations (minimum via count per area) are flagged in areas with high signal pin density, often near macros.
DRC violations are not random – they cluster around the same macro-adjacent channels that showed congestion in the routing stage.

candidate_causes.cause: Insufficient track utilization in a specific layer due to a high density of long parallel nets, leading to spacing violations.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Run a layer‑by‑layer track usage heatmap; if the violating layer has >85% track utilization in that area, and the spacing rule is tight (e.g., min spacing 0.1µm), confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Spread nets to adjacent layers, or increase the area of the block, or change the wiring pitch (if allowed).

candidate_causes.cause: Antenna effect – long metal segments connected to gate oxide are accumulating charge during plasma etching, exceeding antenna ratio limits.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Extract antenna ratio per net from the DRC report; if nets with > allowable ratio have no diode, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Insert antenna diodes at the gate inputs, or jumper the long segment using a higher metal layer (break and route up) to reduce the accumulated area.

candidate_causes.cause: Via density violations occur because the standard cells have limited pin access (e.g., only one metal layer for pin connection) causing many vias on adjacent tracks.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check the cell pin access map; if violating vias are all on the same cell rows, confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Switch to a cell library with better pin access, or add via arrays manually, or rotate the cell orientation to use different layers.

candidate_causes.cause: Signal routing is forced to use a lower metal layer due to high macro blockage on upper layers, leading to local density violations on that lower layer.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Compare the DRC violation map with the macro/blockage map; if violations appear only in areas where upper metal layers are blocked (e.g., by power stripes or macros), confirm.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Reserve more tracks on upper layers by reducing power stripe density or repositioning macro pins.

candidate_causes.cause: The DRC rule deck is overly conservative for the corner (e.g., using worst‑case spacing), and the violations disappear with a less restrictive rule set.
candidate_causes.distinguishing_check: Check if the violations are just at the minimum spacing (exactly the rule limit) and are all of the same type; try relaxing to the foundry's recommended not mandatory rule.
candidate_causes.typical_fix: Update the rule deck to the correct corner, or negotiate waivers with the foundry.

ordering_rationale: Check antenna first (easiest to fix with diodes/jumpers, and often a known issue), then track utilization per layer (most common in high-density blocks), then via density, then blockage-driven layer forcing, then rule‑deck conservatism – because antenna fixes are cheap and quick.
classic_trap: Re‑routing the entire block when the DRCs are all antenna violations that could have been fixed by adding a single diode per violating net in minutes.
